explain.say: The LNB amplifies the signal and lowers its frequency so it can travel down a cable to the set-top box, which decodes the channels for your TV. Heavy rain can soak up the signal and briefly freeze the picture.

faq.a: The uplink is the signal sent from a large dish on the ground up to the satellite. It uses a different frequency from the downlink coming back, so the satellite can receive and transmit at the same time without interference.
asks: How do TV channels get to the satellite?

faq.q: Why does a satellite dish point at one spot?
faq.a: TV satellites are in geostationary orbit, about 35,786 kilometres above the equator, going round once a day in step with Earth's spin. From the ground they stay in one place in the sky, so the dish never needs to move.

faq.q: What does the LNB on a satellite dish do?
faq.a: LNB stands for low-noise block downconverter. It sits where the dish focuses the signal, amplifies it without adding much noise, and lowers its frequency so it can travel along an ordinary cable.
asks: What is the thing on the arm of a satellite dish?

faq.q: Why does satellite TV cut out in heavy rain?
faq.a: Satellite TV uses very high radio frequencies, around 11 to 12 gigahertz, and raindrops absorb and scatter these waves. In a heavy downpour, the already faint signal can become too weak to decode.

faq.q: What does a set-top box do?
faq.a: It tunes to the channel you choose, decodes the compressed digital video and sound, unlocks paid channels, and sends the picture to your TV.
asks: Why do I need a box for satellite TV?

facts: Geostationary satellites orbit 35,786 kilometres above the equator.
Arthur C. Clarke described using geostationary satellites for worldwide communication in 1945.
